name: Black conservatism in the United States
scope: Black conservatism in the United States as the defining sources describe it: the post-civil-rights movement of African American intellectuals and politicians (Thomas Sowell, Shelby Steele, Glenn Loury, Clarence Thomas, Ward Connerly, Alan Keyes) who stress individual self-reliance, limited government, a free-market approach, Christian and traditional values, and oppose affirmative action and racial preferences, placing little weight on discrimination as a cause of disadvantage (Bankston, EBSCO Research Starters). Broader Black conservative thought from the late eighteenth century on (Eisenstadt, ed.) is included only as far as these sources tie it to the movement. Black voters who are culturally conservative but vote Democratic, and Black officeholders as such, are not included unless the sources tie their views to it.

summary: Black conservatism in the United States is the movement of African American intellectuals and politicians who stress individual self-reliance, limited government, free-market economics and Christian and traditional values. Its defining sources present it as opposing affirmative action and racial preferences and as giving little weight to discrimination as a cause of disadvantage.

Themes searched: race policy, economics, religion, family, abortion; the defining sources that name the subject are short reference entries and catalogue pages, so most themes (government structure, world, ecology, technology, liberty beyond race) found no stated position. Washington and Walter Williams were not tied as key figures for lack of a naming source.
